subject: intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories
parts:
Hi,

I have logit model with two categorical covariates (let's call them A
and B) and a bunch of continuous covariates C. In simple least squares, I
would just drop the first category for each categorical covariate,
define coefficients relative to that, and include an intercept.

However, I have good reasons to impose a multilevel distribution on
each group of coefficients, eg

a_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_a);
b_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
c_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_c);

(The full model is below). I have the following questions:

1. What are the best practices for coding this kind of model in Stan, in
terms of sampling efficiency? Currently, I am including an intercept (a
nuisance parameter) -- strictly speaking, the coefficients for A and B
are not identified per se, so I transform them relative to the first one
each. I found that this gives rather efficient samples, but I am
wondering what is recommended. Textbook discussions of similar models
that use Gibbs sampling consider various other techniques to enhance
convergence, but it looks like Stan works fine without them, relative
n_eff of the model below is about 30-90%.

2. I avoid constructing the monster design matrix and use a loop instead
for categorical covariates, then add the continuous covariates using a
matrix product (see below), is this the recommended way?

3. Any other remarks would be appreciated -- this is a stylized version
but the full model has more categorical covariates so I would rather try
to work towards something that samples efficiently, even if that means
more complicated code.

Thanks,

Tamas

PS.: Stylized model and Rstan code for simulating data are attached.

> c_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_c);

>
> 1. What are the best practices for coding this kind of model in Stan, in
> terms of sampling efficiency? Currently, I am including an intercept (a
> nuisance parameter) -- strictly speaking, the coefficients for A and B
> are not identified per se, so I transform them relative to the first one
> each. I found that this gives rather efficient samples, but I am

This is tricky. We've talked about this with Andrew with
no real clear advice on how to put priors on these things
so that the model's both identified and not overly constrained.

The problems it presents are outlined in the problematic posteriors
chapter of the Stan language manual. The addition of a hierarchical
prior for the two coeffs may be solving your issue because you
center both around 0 and there are other terms in the equation
helping to control matters.

Gelman and Hill recommend normalizing this way for Gibbs
samplers, as you point out, but I'm not convinced it even makes sense
there given that you're still trying to sample from an improper posterior
(at least if you don't put priors on the coeffs). Andrew assures
me it's OK, but doesn't think it's worth formalizing now that we're
not using Gibbs.

There's a new section in the 2.5 manual in the problematic
posteriors section called "mitigating the invariances", which
describes some strategies to remediate non-identifiability, which
you get with this part of your model:

for (i in 1:N) {
x[i] <- a_coeff[a[i]] + b_coeff[b[i]];
}
y ~ bernoulli_logit(intercept + x + c * c_coeff);

I'm surprised the model you attached worked so well in Stan. Is
that the n_eff for parameters, or for the normalized coeffs? If
everything declared as a parameter has decent convergence and lp__
also does, you should be OK. There's also a new section in the manual
on convergence --- Michael's been setting me straight on the theory.

> 2. I avoid constructing the monster design matrix and use a loop instead
> for categorical covariates, then add the continuous covariates using a
> matrix product (see below), is this the recommended way?
Yes. That's the most efficient way to write it.

>
> 3. Any other remarks would be appreciated -- this is a stylized version
> but the full model has more categorical covariates so I would rather try
> to work towards something that samples efficiently, even if that means
> more complicated code.

I'd highly recommend doing what you're doing --- starting simple and
working up!

I'm surprised this works well without a prior on intercept. But it's
really all about how well the data constrain the posterior geometry.
You might also want to add priors for the sigma, but if you have
enough data that the posterior's well behaved, it's not necessary.
Stan technically only requires the posterior to be proper.

- Bob

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories
parts:
On Thu, Nov 13 2014, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I'm surprised the model you attached worked so well in Stan. Is
> that the n_eff for parameters, or for the normalized coeffs? If
> everything declared as a parameter has decent convergence and lp__
> also does, you should be OK. There's also a new section in the manual
> on convergence --- Michael's been setting me straight on the theory.

It turns out that the model can be improved, by putting a prior on the
sigma_'s (half-Cauchy) and the intercept (vague normal, see full model
below). For the original, Rhat for lp__ is about 1.1, now it is down to
1.01, the priors for the intercept and the sigmas contribute about half
the improvement, respectively. Statistics for 3 chains:

n_eff Rhat
intercept 83 1.04
a_coeff[1] 75 1.06
a_coeff[2] 72 1.06
a_coeff[3] 75 1.06
b_coeff[1] 81 1.04
b_coeff[2] 83 1.04
b_coeff[3] 93 1.03
c_coeff[1] 345 1.00
c_coeff[2] 280 1.00
sigma_a 173 1.02
sigma_b 186 1.00
sigma_c 223 1.01
normalized_a_coeff[1] 750 NaN
normalized_a_coeff[2] 532 1.00
normalized_a_coeff[3] 422 1.00
normalized_b_coeff[1] 750 NaN
normalized_b_coeff[2] 383 1.00
normalized_b_coeff[3] 382 1.01
lp__ 185 1.01

The good n_eff, of course, is always for the normalized coefficients.

For the list archives, I saved this model at
https://gist.github.com/tpapp/c42f3f3a5f184fcd8403 . I know Cauchy is
excessive, and a uniform would be OK, too.

Thanks for the help!

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories
parts:
On Friday, November 14, 2014 3:54:01 PM UTC+2, Luc Coffeng wrote:
Cool stuff. But what's up with the Rhat = NaN? What does that indicate?
Zero variance, which leads to division by zero when calculating Rhat. In this case, normalized_a_coeff[1] & normalized_b_coeff[1] are always zero.
